nodes.text: Can't Stop analysis: four dice flatten odds, middle columns dominate, consistent probabilistic strategies win, design favors playability.

evidence.text: I recently got introduced to this game called Can't Stop and it got me thinking about probabilities. In this post, I'll take you through probability foundations, column choice, when to stop, continuing vs switching, strategy head-to-heads, and designer balance.

Complete four-dice table: sums 2 to 12 run 171 (13.2%), 302 (23.3%), 461 (35.6%), 580 (44.8%), 727 (56.1%), 834 (64.4%) symmetric. Normalized probability ratio 2-to-7 is 4.88; length ratio is 4.33. Pretty close.

Head-to-head: 38 strategies, 2,500 games per matchup, 3.6M total. FiftyPercentSurvival 69.84% (132,696/190,000); Heuristic(1.5) 66.46%; Heuristic(2.0) 63.26%. Overall first-player advantage +11.18% (P1 wins 55.59%). GreedyUntil1Col bias +31.24%.

Conclusion: four-dice flattens distribution (P7 64.4% vs P2 13.2%, 4.88x vs 6x); combos matter ({6,7,8} 92% vs {2,3,12} 44%); probabilistic strategies dominate; consistency beats speed; P1 advantage 55.59%; forced-move rule compensates imbalance; perfect balance unnecessary.

nodes.text: Roll four dice, pair freely, advance three active markers; bust loses the turn's progress.

evidence.text: The rules are straightforward: roll four dice, pair them up however you want, move your markers. You can keep rolling as long as you want, but if you can't move any of your three active markers, you lose everything gained that turn.
The board has columns numbered 2 through 12, with lengths: 2 and 12: 3 steps; 3 and 11: 5; 4 and 10: 7; 5 and 9: 9; 6 and 8: 11; 7: 13. You need to complete three columns to win.

nodes.text: Columns 2-12 have lengths 3-5-7-9-11-13-11-9-7-5-3; complete three columns to win.

evidence.text: The board has columns numbered 2 through 12, with lengths: 2 and 12: 3 steps; 3 and 11: 5; 4 and 10: 7; 5 and 9: 9; 6 and 8: 11; 7: 13. You need to complete three columns to win.

nodes.text: Forced-move rule: chosen pairing forces ALL its legal moves, even unwanted ones.

evidence.text: Critical rule: you must take all available moves. If your chosen pairing creates any valid move, you must make ALL legal moves from that pairing, even unwanted ones. Example: on {6,7,8} rolling (1,1,3,4) as 2+7 forces taking BOTH 2 and 7.

nodes.text: (1,1,3,4) as 2+7 on {6,7,8} forces taking both 2 and 7.

nodes.text: Two-dice baseline peaks at 7 with 16.67%, exactly 6x likelier than 2 at 2.78%.

evidence.text: Two-dice baseline table: sums 2..12 have 1,2,3,4,5,6,5,4,3,2,1 ways out of 36 (2.78% to 16.67%). Sum 7 at 16.67% is exactly 6x more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.

nodes.text: Sums 2-12 have 1-2-3-4-5-6-5-4-3-2-1 ways of 36; 1 way versus 6 ordered ways.

evidence.text: Two-dice baseline table: sums 2..12 have 1,2,3,4,5,6,5,4,3,2,1 ways out of 36 (2.78% to 16.67%). Sum 7 at 16.67% is exactly 6x more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
Quick proof: P(sum 2) = 1/6 x 1/6 = 1/36; P(sum 7) has 6 ordered ways. If Can't Stop used two dice, column 7 would need to be 6x longer than column 2, but it is only 13/3 approx 4.3x longer.

evidence.text: Quick proof: P(sum 2) = 1/6 x 1/6 = 1/36; P(sum 7) has 6 ordered ways. If Can't Stop used two dice, column 7 would need to be 6x longer than column 2, but it is only 13/3 approx 4.3x longer.

nodes.text: Four-dice pairing offers three pairings and sharply flattens the distribution.

evidence.text: In Can't Stop you roll FOUR dice then pair them up. Example roll 2,3,4,5 gives (2,3)+(4,5)=5 and 9; (2,4)+(3,5)=6 and 8; (2,5)+(3,4)=7 and 7. Just three possible pairings.

Complete four-dice table: sums 2 to 12 run 171 (13.2%), 302 (23.3%), 461 (35.6%), 580 (44.8%), 727 (56.1%), 834 (64.4%) symmetric. Normalized probability ratio 2-to-7 is 4.88; length ratio is 4.33. Pretty close.

nodes.text: P(can make 2) = 171/1296 approx 13.2%, up from two-dice 2.78%.

evidence.text: P(can make a 2) needs at least two 1s: P(zero 1s)=(5/6)^4=625/1296; P(exactly one 1)=500/1296. Therefore P = 1-625/1296-500/1296 = 171/1296 approx 13.2%, way higher than two-dice 2.78%.

nodes.text: P(can make 7) = 834/1296 approx 64.4% via inclusion-exclusion; overlaps 24/1296, triple 0.

evidence.text: P(can make a 7) = 834/1296 approx 64.4% via inclusion-exclusion over A=(1,6), B=(2,5), C=(3,4): each 302/1296, pairwise overlaps 24/1296 each, triple overlap 0. Two-dice P(7) was 16.67%.

nodes.text: Three-column combination choice dominates single-column odds.

evidence.text: You have THREE active columns and bust if you can't hit ANY of them. Columns {6,7,8}: 1193/1296 = 92.0% success. Columns {2,3,12}: 568/1296 = 43.8% success, more likely to bust than succeed.

nodes.text: Continuation usually beats switching, but full quantitative comparison remains open future work.

evidence.text: Should you continue current columns or switch? Mathematics favor continuation in most cases, but forced-move contamination sometimes forces switches. Author notes quantitative always-continue vs switch analysis is open future work.
